identity.title: Powered Industrial Truck Pre-Shift Inspection Log

scan.summary: This is a daily inspection log for a propane-powered Toyota forklift (FL-2) operated at the Portland warehouse. The log documents pre-shift safety inspections per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) covering tires, forks, mast, horn, lights, seat belt, brakes, steering, propane tank, fire extinguisher, data plate, and overhead guard. The company is required to maintain this inspection record as evidence that defective equipment is identified and removed from service before use.
scan.freshness_note: This log covers September 1–18, 2026, and is current as of today (2026-09-29). It is the most recent month-to-date record. A new log or continuation should be started for October 2026.

gaps.title: Missing inspections for September 3–6 and September 12–13
gaps.description: The log shows entries for September 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) requires that powered industrial trucks be examined before being placed in service and shall be examined at least daily. The hour meter shows the truck was in operation on the missing days (hours rose from 4,819 on September 2 to 4,834 on September 7, and from 4,860 on September 11 to 4,873 on September 15), but no inspection records exist for September 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, or 13. This is a gap in documentation required by OSHA.
gaps.fix: Inspect and log the truck before each shift, every day, including weekends and holidays. If the truck was operated on September 3–6 and 12–13 but no shift occurred, document that explicitly (e.g., 'Not in service' or 'Weekend – no operations'). Going forward, do not operate the truck without first recording a pre-shift inspection.
gaps.locator: page 1, pre-shift inspection requirement; pages 1–2, inspection table entries
gaps.quote: Industrial trucks shall be examined before being placed in service and shall not be placed in service if the examination shows any condition adversely affecting the safety of the vehicle. Such examination shall be made at least daily.

gaps.title: Horn defect not removed from service
gaps.description: On September 9, the inspection log shows an 'X' in the Horn column with the operator note 'Horn not working.' However, the truck continued to be used the next day (September 10, inspected by J.R. with all items marked OK, including horn). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) requires that trucks showing a defective condition adversely affecting safety shall not be placed in service, and defects shall be immediately reported and corrected. A non-functioning horn is a safety defect that should have removed the truck from service until repaired.
gaps.fix: When a defect is found during pre-shift inspection, do not place the truck in service. Mark it out of service, notify supervision immediately, document the defect and the date removed from service, repair it, and re-inspect before returning it to use. The September 10 entry should show that either (a) the horn was repaired overnight and re-tested on September 10, or (b) the truck remained out of service.
gaps.quote: shall not be placed in service if the examination shows any condition adversely affecting the safety of the vehicle… Defects when found shall be immediately reported and corrected.

gaps.title: Supervisor review signature missing
gaps.description: The log template includes a line for 'Supervisor review: ______________________ Date: __________', but no supervisor has signed or dated this section. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) does not explicitly require supervisor sign-off, but best practice and many state inspection protocols expect documented supervisory review of inspection records to ensure accountability and that defects are acted upon. The absence of a signature leaves no evidence that a supervisor has reviewed the log or verified that noted defects were corrected.
gaps.fix: Have the appropriate supervisor review the monthly inspection log and sign it with the date. Document the supervisor's name and title. This provides evidence of management oversight and ensures that any defects noted (like the September 9 horn failure) were tracked and corrected before the truck returned to service.
gaps.citation: Oregon OSHA guidance; 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) best practices

conditions.title: Removal of defective equipment from service
conditions.evidence_expected: When an 'X' or defect is marked on the inspection log, the truck must not be placed in service for the next shift. scan.confidence_notes: I am confident about what the document contains and the specific gaps in inspection coverage (missing days and the horn defect not removed from service). I am confident that OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) is the governing standard because the document cites it explicitly. I am confident that the operator names and certification dates are recorded accurately as stated in the document. I am not confident about whether the missing days represent a weekend-only closure or actual operational days, but the hour meter rise between September 2 and September 7 (and between September 11 and September 15) indicates the truck was in use on the missing days. I cannot determine from this log alone why inspections were not documented for those dates—whether inspections occurred but were not logged, or whether the truck was operated without inspection. This is a critical gap. I am moderately confident that the absence of supervisor sign-off is a procedural weakness, though I have not verified whether Oregon-specific OSHA rules explicitly require it. I am not confident about Cascade Specialty Chemicals' overall compliance posture without seeing the maintenance records, repair tickets, or a full month of logs.
